summary: Two iterations have now confirmed that BLIS's 3-objective search space (throughput, TTFT, GPU count) is far easier to solve than expected: ~60% of configurations within each GPU tier achieve near-optimal metrics, so both NSGA-II and random search saturate the Pareto frontier within 50 evaluations. A surprising secondary finding is that TPE performed 7.1% worse than random, actively harming search quality due to incompatibility with BLIS's conditional parameter structure.
key_points: NSGA-II vs. random: no meaningful difference. Both hit 95% of final hypervolume (HV ~8.1M) within the first 50 evaluations. NSGA-II's final HV exceeded random by only 0.02% (8,131,314 vs 8,129,464), within noise. The predicted convergence advantage for NSGA-II (≤200 evals vs random ≥300) did not materialize.

Root cause confirmed: batch size is the only parameter that matters within a GPU tier, and 3 of 5 valid batch sizes (256, 512, and above) achieve tier-optimal metrics. With ~60% of configs already Pareto-optimal per tier, a 50-sample random draw covers all 5 GPU tiers almost certainly — leaving no room for smarter algorithms to add value.

TPE (model-based search) was actively harmful: final HV was 7.1% lower than random (7,552,260 vs 8,129,464). Optuna's multivariate TPE never learned the tp→num_instances dependency, causing it to miss the tp=2/inst=1 configuration entirely and converge to a dominated Pareto front. This is a novel finding: model-based methods can be anti-helpful when the parameter space has conditional dependencies that break modeling assumptions.

What remains unknown: whether any search problem in BLIS is genuinely hard. No tested workload or objective formulation has created a search space where fewer than ~50% of configs achieve near-optimal results. Iteration 3 should target a regime where the optimal configuration is rare — candidates include: (a) workloads with prefix sharing where routing policy actually differentiates performance, (b) a narrow saturation regime (rate just above capacity) where scheduler choice matters, or (c) reducing the eval budget to 50-100 to stress-test algorithm efficiency before the frontier is trivially saturated.

Practical takeaway so far: for BLIS at rate=50 with the default workload, a practitioner can find the full cost-performance Pareto frontier with as few as 15–20 random evaluations. Sophisticated search algorithms provide no benefit and TPE-style methods may hurt.
